product.title: Icelandic 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Icelandic: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Icelandic builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Written for English speakers — each unit tackles one of the points that trip learners up most, from the article glued to the end of the noun to sentences that have no subject at all.

blocks.text: Icelandic is spoken by about **three hundred and eighty thousand people** — fewer than live in a single mid-sized city. Yet this small language has something almost no other language in Europe has: it has **barely changed in a thousand years**. A high-school student in Reykjavík can open a saga written in the 13th century and read it straight off, with no translation. Imagine reading *Beowulf* as easily as the morning paper.

What kept it alive was not luck but a **decision**. Icelanders refuse to borrow foreign words; when something new arrives, they build a word for it out of roots they already have. A telephone is not a *telefón* but a *sími* — an old word for "thread". A computer is not a *computer* but a *tölva*, a blend of "number" and "prophetess". Television is *sjónvarp*, "sight-throwing". A helicopter is *þyrla*, from the verb "to whirl".

For a beginner, that habit is a **double-edged sword**. The downside is obvious: unlike Dutch or German, you can hardly guess a single word from English. The upside is much bigger and rarely mentioned: once you know a few hundred roots, **you can take long words apart on your own**. *Matur* food, *staður* place, so *matstaður* is a restaurant. *Bók* book, *safn* collection, so *bókasafn* is a library. English does the same with words like *bookshop* and *footpath*, so the idea won't feel foreign.

So where is the hard part? In three places, and this course introduces them one after another so they don't pile up: **three noun genders** that decide the form of every word around them, **four cases** that change word endings according to their role in the sentence, and **an article glued to the end of the word** — *bók* a book, *bókin* the book. English has none of the three, apart from traces like *he/him/his*.

The good news is just as real. **Stress always falls on the first syllable** — always, without exception, even in loanwords and foreign names; nothing to memorize the way you must in English or Russian. **There is no future verb form**: "I'm going tomorrow" uses the same form as "I go", much as English says *I leave tomorrow*. Only half hours need care: *hálf níu* is **8:30** — halfway to nine — not British "half nine" (9:30).

blocks.title: Before you start
items: This course asks only one thing of you: **say it out loud**. Icelandic has two letters that are not in the English alphabet (**þ** and **ð**) and a string of sounds that can only be trained with your mouth, not your eyes.
Do one unit per sitting, 20–30 minutes. Five days a week gets you through all twenty units in under two months.
Don't skip the pronunciation chapter on the next pages. The pronunciation guide throughout the course follows the rules explained there, and without them it will mislead you.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *Góða ferð!* — have a good trip.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: Twenty units, each built to settle one of the points that trip learners up most.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, 20 to 30 minutes, and asks nothing of you except a willingness to read out loud.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read only the Icelandic, without glancing below. Only then read the translation.
**Literal translation** — the small line under each sentence. It often sounds odd in English, and that is the point: it shows how Icelandic *really* puts a thought together.
**Notes** — things that are visible in the dialogue but that you may not have noticed.
**Grammar boxes** — the rule you have just seen at work, explained after you have seen it, not before.
**Extra sections** — reference tables, ready-to-use phrases, culture notes.
**Vocabulary** — every new word of the unit, with its pronunciation.
**Exercises** and **answer key** — four groups of questions; do them all before you open the key.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: After finishing a new unit, briefly revisit the unit from **two days ago** and the one from **a week ago** — just read the dialogue out loud, two minutes per unit.
This is not a time-saving tip; it is the only way to keep Unit 3 alive in your head by the time you reach Unit 15.

blocks.text: One warning specific to Icelandic: **don't try to memorize the case tables at the start**. Four cases times three genders times singular and plural times definite and indefinite makes dozens of boxes, and no Icelander ever learned the language from those boxes. This course introduces the cases one at a time — nefnifall (nominative) in Unit 3, þolfall (accusative) in Unit 8, þágufall (dative) in Unit 9, eignarfall (genitive) in Unit 19 — always through sentences you have already seen in use.
If a unit feels heavy, don't spend longer on it; go back over the previous one. Icelandic builds on itself, and almost every "I don't get it" moment is really a gap two units back.

Icelandic writes what it says — but with **an alphabet of its own**, not the English one. Once you know the sound of each letter, you can read any word correctly without a dictionary. That is why this chapter comes first: twenty minutes here saves two months of bad habits.

blocks.title: One rule that holds throughout the course
items: **Stress is ALWAYS on the first syllable.** Always. Even in foreign names and long words: *Reykjavík* → **RAY**-kyah-veek, *sjónvarpið* → **SYOHN**-vahr-pidh. In the "Say it" column the stressed syllable is written in CAPITALS.

The pronunciation guide in this course uses **English-style spelling**, not phonetic symbols. Read it as you would read English, except for the few symbols explained below: **ü**, **ö**, **öi**, **th/dh**, and an **h right after a vowel**.

blocks.title: The three most common vowel traps
items: **au is öi, not ow.** *Laugardagur* (Saturday) is not "law-gar-dagur" but **LÖI-gahr-dah-gür**. This is the number-one mistake for English speakers, whose eyes have read *au* as "aw" or "ow" all their lives.
**u and ú are two completely different sounds.** *hús* (house) is said hoos, while the plain *u* in *sumar* is **ü** with rounded lips. Getting this wrong is not an accent; it is a different word.
**á is not a long a.** *á* is always **ow**: *á* (on, at) is said "ow", *sár* (wound) is said "sowr".

rows: voiceless **th** — tongue tip at the teeth, breath flowing, throat silent. Like *th* in "thing".
voiced **dh** — tongue in the same place, but the throat vibrates. Like *th* in "the".

blocks.text: These two letters are not decoration: replacing **þ** with *t* or **ð** with *d* makes you sound foreign at once, and in some words it changes the meaning. In the "Say it" column, **th** always means þ (*thin*) and **dh** always means ð (*this*). The quickest drill: put your hand on your throat and say *þ* — it must **not** vibrate; then *ð* — it must vibrate.

blocks.title: A spelling rule that helps
items: **þ only appears at the START of a word.** *þú*, *það*, *þrír*, *þakka*. If a "th" sound comes in the middle or at the end of a word, it is always spelled **ð**: *góður*, *maður*, *að*.
So you don't need to memorize which letter goes in which word — its position decides.

blocks.title: A breath before double consonants — 'preaspiration'
items: **pp, tt, kk** are not said as long consonants but with **a short puff of breath in front**: they sound like *hp*, *ht*, *hk*. In the "Say it" column this breath is shown as an **h right after the vowel** (*ahh*, *ehh*, *ihh*, *awh*…).
*detta* (to fall) → DEHH-tah, not "det-ta". *ekki* (not) → EHH-kih. *upp* (up) → ühp.
The same rule applies to **pl, pn, tl, tn, kl, kn**: *vopn* (weapon) → vawhpn, *epli* (apple) → EHHP-lih.
English has nothing quite like it. Don't worry if you can't do it yet — it never changes the meaning of a word, only your accent. What matters is that you **recognize it when you hear it**.

blocks.text: Sentences with no subject

blocks.title: The five most common mistakes, and how to avoid them
items: **Putting the verb in third place.** Icelandic locks the verb in **second place**: *Í dag fer ég heim*, not *Í dag ég fer heim* ("Today I go home"). If something else comes first, the verb jumps ahead of the subject.
**Translating "I like" as *ég líka*.** The form is *mér líkar* — "I" becomes the indirect object, not the subject. The same goes for *mér finnst* and *mig langar*.
**Thinking *vil* means "will".** *Vil* means **want**. "Will" is *ætla að* or the ordinary present tense.
**Thinking *má ekki* means "don't have to".** *Má ekki* means **must not** — a prohibition. "Don't have to" is *þarf ekki*.
**Forgetting the noun's gender when choosing a number.** *Einn strákur*, *ein stelpa*, *eitt barn* — three forms of one number, and the numbers 1–4 all work like that.

blocks.text: These thirty verbs cover most of everyday conversation. The þátíð column gives the *ég* form; the sagnbót column is the form used after *hafa*.

If you have reached this page after working through all twenty units, you now hold the whole framework of Icelandic: three genders, four cases, three tenses, and sentences without a subject. What you don't have yet is not new rules but **flying hours**.
What to do next

items: **Reread all twenty dialogues from the start, without looking at the translations.** Units 1 to 5 will now feel almost like English. That is the most honest measure of progress.

**Listen to RÚV.** Its radio and TV news can be streamed from outside Iceland, and the weather forecast is perfect practice material: a small vocabulary, repeated every day, and all of it is in Unit 19.
**Move on to plural nouns and cases inside longer sentences** — that is what A2 is about. You already have the framework; only the tables get bigger.
**Write five sentences about your day, every day.** Five, not fifty. It's the consistency that works, not the amount.

blocks.title: One very Icelandic thing
items: Because there are only 380,000 speakers, almost every Icelander speaks English — and they will **switch to English automatically** the moment they hear your accent. That's courtesy, not rejection.

One sentence that stops it: *Má ég reyna á íslensku?* — "May I try in Icelandic?" Hardly any Icelander will say no; outsiders so rarely learn their language that your effort comes across as a compliment.

blocks.text: *Til hamingju og góða ferð!* — Congratulations, and have a good trip.
